answer.label: Not Virginia Woolf — actually screenwriter David Hare
answer.sourceLine: This line never appears in Virginia Woolf's novels, essays, diaries, or letters. It was written by screenwriter David Hare for the 2002 film adaptation of The Hours, where the fictionalized Virginia Woolf (played by Nicole Kidman) says it to her husband Leonard at a train station — and it isn't in Michael Cunningham's original 1998 novel either.

source.excerpt: You cannot find peace by avoiding life, Leonard.
trail: The Virginia Woolf Society of Great Britain confirms this line “appears nowhere in Woolf’s published works” and files it under Not Woolf but Hare ↗.
The words were written by screenwriter David Hare for the 2002 film; his published screenplay is catalogued at the Internet Archive ↗.
As delivered on screen, Virginia says “You cannot find peace by avoiding life, Leonard” — confirmed by a full film transcript ↗.
Fan sites such as Quotes.net ↗ catalog the line as movie dialogue even while mislabeling it a Woolf quote, showing how the misattribution spread.
source.excerptNote: As delivered in the finished 2002 film. The Faber and Faber 2008 published screenplay prints the line as “You do not find peace by avoiding life, Leonard.”

misattribution.heading: Often misattributed
misattribution.intro: This is one of the most widely shared “Virginia Woolf” quotes online — and it isn't hers.

items.why: The Virginia Woolf Society of Great Britain ↗ states the line “appears nowhere in Woolf's published works” and traces it instead to screenwriter David Hare.

Quote sites including Goodreads ↗ credit the line to Cunningham's 1998 novel The Hours, but the Woolf Society notes it is “not in Michael Cunningham's novel” either — Hare wrote it specifically for his film script.

misattribution.truthLine: The words belong to screenwriter David Hare ↗, invented for Nicole Kidman's fictionalized Virginia Woolf in the 2002 film adaptation of The Hours.

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: The line captures something that feels emotionally true to Woolf — her insistence on engaging with London life rather than retreating into invalidism in the suburbs — which is likely why audiences and quote sites accepted it as authentically hers.
But it was written eight decades after Woolf's 1941 death, as dialogue for a fictionalized version of her voice in a Hollywood adaptation, not copied from anything Woolf herself wrote.
context.detailsSummary: Why does the exact wording differ slightly across sources?
detailsBody: The line as delivered in the 2002 film reads “You cannot find peace by avoiding life, Leonard,” matching the film transcript ↗ and the wording that spread online.
The published screenplay (Faber and Faber, 2008, p. 96), cited by the Virginia Woolf Society ↗, prints it slightly differently: “You do not find peace by avoiding life, Leonard.”
context.pull: Powerful film dialogue is not the same thing as a line from Woolf's own hand.
